issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent physical bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on anger, distrust, hypervigilance, and media avoidance after police violence but contains no corroborating threat or memory content about ongoing somatic injury, pain, disability, or bodily fragility. It stands out as a different trauma consequence than the remainder of the formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling used for excitement/distracting is weakly connected to the rest of the selected profile. The dominant formulation is Threat ↔ Negative Appraisals with trauma-memory-linked fear/anger and avoidance of feelings/media. Gambling for excitement does not clearly address the specific threat, memory, or appraisal pattern represented elsewhere, making it the least coherent maladaptive strategy in this set.

vignette:
Karim is fifty-six and works as a social media manager for a regional news outlet. The violence happened on a Tuesday night, after a long shift monitoring trending feeds. A police officer pulled him over for a broken taillight, and within minutes Karim was on the ground, his face pressed into the asphalt, a knee grinding into his back. He tasted blood from his split lip-metal and salt-and felt an explosion of rage that he could not act on. When the officer finally let him go without charges, Karim drove home in silence, his hands shaking on the wheel. He had not fought back; he had stayed still, said "yes sir," and that felt like a betrayal of everything he believed about himself.

In the weeks that followed, the world rearranged itself. Karim came to believe that people are not what they seem, that danger hides behind uniforms and polite routines. He was certain the world is a dangerous place, and that he had acted in ways that go against who he is-that he had been weak, complicit. These appraisals became the lens through which he saw every interaction. He began to feel a constant thrum of fear and shame, and even at home, behind locked doors, he could not relax. Before sitting down in any room, he would note where the doors were, which windows opened, which direction led to the street.

His job required him to scroll through dozens of news clips and user-generated videos each day. The sight of a police cruiser or a raised voice in a clip would spike his heart rate, and he learned to avoid entire categories of content-anything about police brutality, protests, even crime dramas. He told himself he was being practical, but he also began to avoid strong feelings altogether, staying emotionally flat because he was afraid that one sharp emotion might tip him into the rage that still lived under his ribs. The avoidance, however, only made the memory more stubborn. When the taste of blood returned-sometimes without warning, in the middle of a meeting or while brushing his teeth-he would push the memory away before it could fully form, but the rage always arrived first, hot and familiar, and then he would be scanning the room again, checking for exits, unable to focus on anything else.

Over months, these patterns tightened. The threat he felt-the constant scanning, the inability to relax, the sense that he was never truly safe-confirmed his original appraisals: yes, the world is dangerous, and no, he cannot trust anyone. Each time he avoided a feeling or a video, he reinforced the belief that he could not handle what was inside him, that he had become someone who acted against his own values by staying silent and passive. The very strategies he used to protect himself made the memory more intrusive and the rage more volatile, and that in turn kept his threat system lit up every hour of the day.

His wife noticed he had stopped watching television with her, that he flinched at the sound of sirens, that he checked the street before leaving for work. At work, his supervisor mentioned that his curated feeds had become narrow, too safe. Karim knew he was falling behind, but the thought of accidentally seeing a video of police violence made his mouth go dry. He came to therapy because his sleep had fractured and his wife had said, gently, that she missed him. What frightened him most was not the memory itself, but the possibility that the rage he felt on recall might one day erupt in a way he could not control-that he might become the person the officer had assumed he was.
